newsitem.title: CHINA: China urges U.S., Iraq to halt military action.
newsitem.headline: China urges U.S., Iraq to halt military action.

text.p: China on Thursday called on Washington and Baghdad to halt military action in the Gulf, saying Beijing was strongly displeased with U.S. cruise missile attacks on Iraq this week.

"We ask the parties concerned to halt their military actions...and work towards a reasonable and a just settlement of the questions left over from the Gulf crisis," Foreign Ministry spokesman Shen Guofang told a regular news briefing in Beijing.

"We feel deep regret and want to express our strong displeasure at the missile attack once again by the United States against Iraq, which has inflicted casualties upon Iraq's civilians and caused property losses," Shen said.
U.S. ships and planes fired 44 cruise missiles in less than 24 hours on Tuesday in two waves of attacks on targets in southern Iraq.
Washington said the attacks were launched to punish Baghdad for a weekend military drive into a Western-protected safe haven for Kurdish groups in northern Iraq.
U.S. President Bill Clinton said the cruise missile attacks against Iraq had further weakened Iraqi President Saddam Hussein and accomplished immediate U.S. goals.
Pentagon officials denied Iraqi claims on Wednesday that the United States had fired a third volley of missiles at military and civilian facilities in the Baghdad area.
Shen said the attacks only worsened tensions in the Gulf.

"The all too frequent use of force against a sovereign state has not only seriously violated the relevant norms of international law and worsened the situation and tensions in that region concerned, but will also give rise to grave consequences," he said.
"The Chinese government hereby reiterates that the sovereign and territorial integrity of Iraq must be respected," Shen said.

On Wednesday, China's official Xinhua news agency accused the United States of using the missile strikes to bolster its military presence in the Gulf and to boost President Clinton's image in an election year.
